name: Political Polarization in a Digital Era
description:
A democratic society is characterized with a complexity of social divisions, but the nature of humans to cluster in groups of like-minded individuals often leads to conflict within the society. Nevertheless, it is a “natural conflict”, as the tendency for people to unite around common identities has always existed, at least based on the evidence we have. It is natural for humans to associate, socialize and be more comfortable with those having similar belief systems. This process of selectivity, taking place in democratic societies, is contradictory in a sense that it has as much a uniting as it has a divisive utility. For decades, political scientists have been pointing out the commendable quality of the American democracy to unite its citizens despite their differences. While the rule of law in democratic systems such as the United States provides for the decrease in inter-group violence, the citizens’ political attitudes remain divided and, at times, diametrical, even polar opposites. The rule of law may provide for the lack of observed animosity between the opposing groups, but it has not resulted in a disappearance of social divisions. Depending on the austerity of social cleavages, voters in democracies sort themselves along the lines of party politics with a relatively higher or lower level of cross-cutting identities.
Nevertheless, the exact definition of political definition is somewhat multifaceted. It may refer to animosity between politicians from opposing parties, between the members of the public based on different political positions, or it may simply mean a perception that either of the two is actually taking place. Throughout this course, the students will learn to differentiate various types of political polarization in consolidated and hybrid democracies, will obtain insights into the origin of modern political polarization and, most importantly, will be able to place the modern examples of polarization in the context of inrceasing digitalization and proliferation of social media.
